```{r setup, include = FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(collapse = TRUE, comment = "#>")
library(fivenumMeta)
has_mm <- requireNamespace("metamedian", quietly = TRUE)   # the data
has_mf <- requireNamespace("metafor", quietly = TRUE)      # the REML fits
has_meta <- has_mm && has_mf
num <- function(x, d = 1) {
  if (has_meta) formatC(x, format = "f", digits = d) else "(not run)"
}
```

## The problem, and what this package does

Many studies in a meta-analysis report a median with the quartiles, or with the minimum and
the maximum, instead of the sample mean and sample standard deviation (SD). The established estimators (Wan,
Luo and Shi, and the best linear unbiased estimators from the reported values) impute population
mean and standard deviation parameters from such a summary. In the pooling stage of a meta-analysis, such imputed mean and SD estimators are often treated as the sample mean and
sample SD, with the naive standard errors of the sample mean and sample SD. However, the imputed estimators are generally less precise than the sample estimators. Thus their variations/uncertainties should be accounted for.

This package computes, under normality, how much less precise. The standard deviation of the
imputed mean is $C_\mu(n)\,\sigma$ and that of the imputed SD is $C_\sigma(n)\,\sigma$, with
factors that depend on the sample size, on which values were reported, on the estimator and on
the definition of the sample quantiles, and not on the data. The package computes the factors
exactly from the means and covariances of the normal order statistics.
It returns the plug-in standard errors $C_\mu(n)\,\hat\sigma$ and $C_\sigma(n)\,\hat\sigma$ that
belong in the weights of a meta-analysis.

```{r factors, echo = FALSE}
k2 <- inflation_factors(25, "S2")
k1 <- inflation_factors(25, "S1")
k3 <- inflation_factors(25, "S3")
k1b <- inflation_factors(1001, "S1")
pct <- function(x) formatC(100 * (x - 1), format = "f", digits = 0)
```

At a sample size of 25, the standard deviation of the imputed mean exceeds $\sigma/\sqrt n$
by `r pct(k2[["kappa_mu"]])`% when the three quartiles are reported, by
`r pct(k1[["kappa_mu"]])`% when the minimum, median and maximum are reported, and by
`r pct(k3[["kappa_mu"]])`% when all five values are. The standard deviation of the
imputed SD exceeds that of a sample SD by `r pct(k2[["kappa_sigma"]])`%,
`r pct(k1[["kappa_sigma"]])`% and `r pct(k3[["kappa_sigma"]])`% in the same three cases.
With only the minimum, median and maximum reported, the excess grows with the sample size, to
`r pct(k1b[["kappa_mu"]])`% and `r pct(k1b[["kappa_sigma"]])`% at a sample size of 1001.

### The evidence on a public data set

The example data set comes from the meta-analysis of Katzenschlager et al. (2021) of the age
of COVID-19 patients who died against those who survived, shipped with the `metamedian` package
as `dat.age`: 51 studies, two groups each, of which 29 report the quartiles and 22 a mean and
SD. The call below imputes the mean and SD of each group where they are missing, keeps the
sample ones where they are not, and appends the difference of means (nonsurvivors minus
survivors) with its standard error under the naive rule and under the exact factors. The
quartiles are taken under R's default definition (type 7), the package's default. A study that
states another definition is given its `type`.

```{r example, eval = has_meta}
d <- se_imputed_diff(
  data     = metamedian::dat.age,   # one row per study
  suffixes = c(".g1", ".g2"),       # the two groups' suffixes, group 1 first
  version  = "blue"                 # the BLUE (default) or "wan_luo_shi"
)
str(d)   # the input columns, each group's output columns, the difference
table(d$scenario.g1)
range(d$se_mu.g1[d$scenario.g1 == "S2"] / d$se_naive.g1[d$scenario.g1 == "S2"])
```

The result keeps every input column and appends, for each group with its suffix, the scenario
read off the row, the imputed or sample mean and SD, and the three standard errors, then the
difference `yi` with its standard errors `sei_naive` and `sei`. The section "Where to look
afterwards" defines each column. `pool_imputed()` pools the studies under the naive and the
exact standard errors side by side, with the common-effect model by default:

```{r pooled, eval = has_meta}
fit <- pool_imputed(d)
fit
```

The estimates, standard errors and interval limits are in years and $I^2$ is in percent. For
the random-effects model, `metafor` takes the same columns (here with REML):

```{r metafor, eval = has_meta}
re_naive <- metafor::rma(yi, sei = sei_naive, data = d)   # random effects, REML
re_exact <- metafor::rma(yi, sei = sei, data = d)
row <- function(fit) {
  c(estimate = as.numeric(fit$b), se = fit$se, ci.lb = fit$ci.lb,
    ci.ub = fit$ci.ub, tau2 = fit$tau2, I2 = fit$I2)
}
round(rbind(`naive SE` = row(re_naive), `exact SE` = row(re_exact)), 3)
```

$\tau^2$ is in years squared.

```{r numbers, echo = FALSE, eval = has_meta}
imp <- d$scenario.g1 == "S2"
w_n <- fit$weights$naive; w_e <- fit$weights$exact   # percent
share_n <- sum(w_n[imp]) / 100; share_e <- sum(w_e[imp]) / 100
wr <- range(w_e[imp] / w_n[imp])
r_se <- range(d$se_mu.g1[imp] / d$se_naive.g1[imp])
ce_se <- fit$fits[, "se"]; names(ce_se) <- rownames(fit$fits)
# the prose below states these directions, so the build stops if the data no
# longer support them
stopifnot(r_se[1] > 1, wr[2] < 1, share_e < share_n,
          ce_se["exact"] > ce_se["naive"], re_exact$tau2 < re_naive$tau2)
```
Three things can be read off the output. First, for every study that reports quartiles, the
exact standard error of its imputed mean is `r num(100 * (r_se[1] - 1))`% to
`r num(100 * (r_se[2] - 1))`% larger than the naive one, so such a study carries
`r num(100 * (1 - wr[2]), 0)`% to `r num(100 * (1 - wr[1]), 0)`% less weight. Under the
common-effect model, the share of the weight on the quartile studies falls from
`r num(100 * share_n)`% to `r num(100 * share_e)`%, and the pooled standard error rises
by `r num(100 * (ce_se["exact"] / ce_se["naive"] - 1))`%. Second, under the random-effects
model the pooled difference moves by
`r num(100 * abs(as.numeric(re_exact$b - re_naive$b)) / re_naive$se)`% of its standard
error, and the standard error itself by `r num(100 * abs(re_exact$se / re_naive$se - 1))`%, because
the between-study variance dominates the total there ($I^2$ of `r num(re_naive$I2, 0)`%). Third, $\tau^2$ is smaller under the exact standard errors, `r num(re_exact$tau2)`
against `r num(re_naive$tau2)`, because larger within-study variances leave less of the spread
of the estimates to be read as heterogeneity.

```{r not-run, echo = FALSE, results = "asis"}
# printed only when an optional package was missing at build time, so the
# numbers above read "(not run)"; it names the one that was missing
if (!has_meta) {
  miss <- c("metamedian", "metafor")[!c(has_mm, has_mf)]
  one <- length(miss) == 1
  cat("The package", if (one) "" else "s", " ", paste(miss, collapse = " and "),
      if (one) " was" else " were", " not available when this vignette was ",
      "built, so the example did not run and its numbers read ",
      "\"(not run)\". Install ", if (one) "it" else "both", " and rebuild the ",
      "vignette, or run the calls above in a session that has ",
      if (one) "it" else "them", ".\n", sep = "")
}
```

The calls to use: `se_imputed_diff()` for two groups per row, `se_imputed_df()` for one, and
`pool_imputed()` to pool, with `version = "blue"` (the default). `version = "wan_luo_shi"`
gives the estimators of Wan, Luo and Shi instead, for comparability with an earlier analysis.
For a meta-analysis of SDs, `se_imputed_diff(..., measure = "lnVR")` gives the log
variability ratio of the two groups with its two standard errors, as the second vignette
shows.

## Setup: the columns and the scenarios

`se_imputed_df()` takes one row per study and reads these columns, each named by an argument
with the default shown, with a `suffix` appended for data sets that carry two groups side by
side:

| Argument | Default column | Holds |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `n` | `n` | the sample size |
| `min`, `max` | `min`, `max` | the minimum and the maximum |
| `q1`, `med`, `q3` | `q1`, `med`, `q3` | the first quartile, the median, the third quartile |
| `mean`, `sd` | `mean`, `sd` | the sample mean and SD, where a study gives them |

A column that the data set does not have, or an argument set to `NULL`, counts as absent for
every row, and a missing value counts as absent for that row. The scenario of a row is read
off the values present: all five give $S_3$; the three quartiles give $S_2$; the minimum,
median and maximum give $S_1$; a sample mean and SD with no summary give "sample", whose
standard error is sd / sqrt(n); and a mean with the minimum and the maximum and no SD gives
"mean_range", where the mean is kept and the SD is imputed from the range. A row with both a
summary and a sample mean and SD follows `prefer`, which is `"sample"` by default because the
sample statistics are the direct measurement. A row with none of these, with a missing sample
size, with values out of order, or whose standard errors would be zero (a sample SD of zero, a
summary whose values are all equal) gets `NA` in every output column and is named in one
warning with its reason. The
function does not stop, so the whole table comes back. Output columns left by an earlier call are replaced.

The factors are computed exactly at every sample size. At $n = 4Q + 1$ the reported
quartiles are single order statistics. At any other sample size each reported quantile is a
fixed combination of two neighboring order statistics, by R's default definition (type 7 of
`quantile()`) unless the argument `type` names another, and the factors there depend on that
definition. The closed-form shortcut formulas of Appendix A are within half a percent of the
exact factors at every sample size $n = 4Q + 1$ from 5 to 1001.

## Where to look afterwards

Each group's output columns carry its suffix.

| Column | What it holds |
| --- | --- |
| `scenario` | `"S1"`, `"S2"`, `"S3"`, `"sample"` or `"mean_range"`, as read off the row |
| `mu_hat`, `sigma_hat` | the imputed mean and SD, or the sample ones |
| `se_naive` | $\hat\sigma/\sqrt n$, the standard error that treats the imputed mean as a sample mean |
| `se_mu` | $C_\mu(n)\,\hat\sigma$, the exact plug-in standard error of the imputed mean (for a sample mean, sd / sqrt(n)) |
| `se_sigma` | $C_\sigma(n)\,\hat\sigma$, the exact plug-in standard error of the imputed SD (for a sample SD, the standard deviation of a sample SD under normality with the SD plugged in) |
| `version_used` | `"blue"`, `"wan_luo_shi"` or `"sample"` |
| `exact` | `TRUE` for a row with an imputed value, whose factors are computed exactly at its sample size, `NA` for a sample row |

`se_imputed_diff()` adds `yi`, the effect of the study, with `sei_naive` and `sei`, its
standard errors from the naive and from the exact standard errors, the two groups' variances
added. By default the effect is the difference of the two means (group 1 minus group 2), and
`measure = "lnVR"` makes it the log variability ratio, the log of the SD of group 1 over the SD
of group 2. `pool_imputed()` pools these columns under both standard errors, and
`metafor::rma(yi, sei = sei)` takes them as they are.

The vignette `two-meta-analyses` reproduces the two meta-analyses of Wu, Shi and Tong (2026): a
meta-analysis of means in which studies report the median and the range, on the data set
`vitd` that ships with the package, and a meta-analysis of SDs in which studies report the
quartiles, on this data set.

## Appendix A. The factors by scenario

`inflation_factors()` returns the ratio of the standard deviation of the imputed mean to
that of the sample mean, $\kappa_\mu(n) = C_\mu(n)\sqrt n$, and the ratio of the standard
deviation of the imputed SD to that of the sample SD, $\kappa_\sigma(n)$, for the best linear
unbiased estimator (BLUE, the default) or the estimators of Wan, Luo and Shi
(`version = "wan_luo_shi"`).

```{r table}
grid <- c(5, 25, 101, 1001)
tab <- sapply(c("S1", "S2", "S3"),
              function(sc) sapply(grid, function(n) inflation_factors(n, sc)))
rownames(tab) <- paste0(rep(c("kappa_mu", "kappa_sigma"), length(grid)),
                        ", n = ", rep(grid, each = 2))
round(tab, 3)
```

Under $S_2$ both factors are nearly constant in the sample size. Under $S_1$ both grow with
it: $\kappa_\mu(n)$ toward its limit $\sqrt{\pi/2}$, about 25% above one, and
$\kappa_\sigma(n)$ without bound, because $C_\sigma(n)$ decays only like $1/\log n$ there
while the standard deviation of a sample SD decays like $1/\sqrt n$. Under $S_3$ the extremes help at small sample sizes and the
factors move toward those of $S_2$ as the sample grows. The closed-form shortcut formulas
`c_mu_shortcut()` and `c_sigma_shortcut()` give the factors $C_\mu(n)$ and $C_\sigma(n)$
without the integration, for a reader without this package and for comparison:

```{r shortcut}
c(exact = c_mu(25, "S2"), shortcut = c_mu_shortcut(25, "S2"))
c(exact = c_sigma(25, "S2"), shortcut = c_sigma_shortcut(25, "S2"))
```

## Appendix B. One study at a time

`se_imputed()` takes one study's reported values and sample size.

```{r one}
se_imputed(c(q1 = 10, med = 12, q3 = 15), n = 25, scenario = "S2")
```

The imputed mean is the median pulled a little toward the mid-quartile range, the imputed SD
is a multiple of the interquartile range, and the exact standard error of the mean exceeds the
naive one by the factor of the table above at $n = 25$ under $S_2$.
